claims.text: Constraining atomic or precursor mobility governs the formation of noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles through stochastic principles.
For systems containing five or more elements, constrained mobility makes elemental incorporation a kinetically controlled stochastic process.
Constrained mobility minimizes diffusion-driven elemental segregation.
Limited mobility forces random mixing of reduced metal species and favors homogeneous single-phase nanoparticles over phase-separated structures.
The proposed starting material can be a solid or solution-based mixture of noble-metal precursors containing at least five elements.
Rapid heating or reduction followed by controlled cooling can inhibit free diffusion of reduced atoms during nanoparticle nucleation.
Single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticles can form at low temperature while precursor mobility is inhibited.
A transient high-temperature regime with controlled cooling limits precursor mobility while still allowing precursor reduction.
Reduced atomic clusters with limited diffusion act as spatially distributed nucleation sites.
Restricted mobility makes the sequence of reduction events effectively random.
Stochastic nucleation randomly incorporates multiple metal species into nuclei and thereby suppresses segregation pathways.
Reduction kinetics, including the time each precursor takes to reach steady state, determine whether quinary noble-metal nanocrystals are homogeneous alloys or compositionally structured particles.
Relative to a higher-mobility baseline, inhibited mobility will produce more uniform, single-phase nanoparticles with less phase separation and elemental segregation.
Under standard higher-mobility synthesis conditions, sequential reduction often promotes phase separation or elemental segregation.
The mechanism applies primarily to systems with five or more metals undergoing solid- or quasi-solid-phase reduction.
The mechanism is not expected to apply to binary or simple alloys because cooperative reduction dynamics dominate in those systems.
The mechanism is not expected to apply when inherently rapid reduction kinetics overwhelm mobility constraints.
X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption measurements can follow phase formation in this noble-metal HEA system.
TEM-EDS can assess elemental homogeneity and segregation in the proposed comparison.
